source.title_on_document: Fostering Innovation with Generative AI: A Study on Human-AI Collaborative Ideation and User Anonymity

supplement.holds: No supplement or online appendix is referred to in the complete document, and none is appended. The app-source repository is linked in Section 3 (PDF p. 2, printed p. 343); it is not identified as a supplement.

paper_design_summary: Master's students used AI-deation during a course group-work session, with 29 consenting participants analyzed. Participants were randomly divided between an AI collaborator supplying ideas plus an AI idea editor, and the same editor without the collaborator, for three rounds of three minutes. Participants rated each idea for novelty and usefulness, and two authors rated innovation; the paper also compares the AI collaborator's own ideas with participants' ideas.

studies.label: Classroom group ideation: AI collaborator plus idea editor versus idea editor alone

assignment.what_was_assigned: Presence of an AI collaborator supplying two new ideas per round versus no collaborator; both conditions used the LLM idea editor. The paper says participants were randomly divided, supporting the reported individual assignment code, but does not describe the randomization procedure or its relationship to the course groups.
assignment.quote: In this experiment, we randomly divided the participants into two conditions.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 346), end of Section 4

arms.name: Human and AI collaborator
arms.description: AI-deation with the GPT-3.5 Turbo idea editor and an AI collaborator supplying two new ideas per round; the collaborator supplied 48 ideas, 38.71% of ideas in this condition. Sources: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 344), Section 3; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 346), Sections 4-5.

arms.name: Human-only (baseline)
arms.description: AI-deation without the AI collaborator; submitted ideas were still reformulated by the same LLM idea editor. Sources: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 344), Section 3.1; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 346), end of Section 4.

participants.exclusions: 32 students attended and 29 consented (PDF p. 4, printed p. 345, Section 4); 29 were analyzed, 13 in control and 16 in treatment (PDF p. 5, printed p. 346, Section 5). The count randomized and the timing of consent relative to assignment are not reported. Questionnaire sample sizes are not substituted for the creative-output sample: the text reports t(27) and t(28), not explicit analysis counts for those items (PDF p. 5, Section 5.1). The pool-of-ideas open-question passage reports 19 out of 25 respondents (PDF p. 7, printed p. 348, Section 6).
participants.who: Master's students in General Management taking a 6-ECTS course on information system design; 9 male, 23 female among the 32 attendees; most not native English speakers.
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 346), Sections 4 and 5; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 345), Section 4, attendance and consent

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-3.5 Turbo (OpenAI) for both components; the cited API reference specifies gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 (PDF p. 3, printed p. 344, Section 3; PDF p. 10, printed p. 351, References).
ai_tool.how_used: The AI collaborator receives the problem and the group's existing solutions. Figure 2 requests one disruptive solution per prompt, limited to 200 characters; the actual experiment used two new AI suggestions per round (PDF p. 3, printed p. 344, Figure 2; PDF p. 5, printed p. 346, Section 4). Suggestions enter the pool at the end of a round and become visible in the following round (PDF p. 4, printed p. 345, Section 3.1). In both arms the idea editor reformulates submitted ideas into neutral language for anonymity (PDF pp. 3-5, Sections 3-4). Use of external AI systems such as ChatGPT before submission was not prevented (PDF p. 5, Section 4).

task.description: Collaborative ideation in the course's Sustainable Development Goal project context. Participants could propose a new idea or build on an existing group idea, with a 200-character limit, and then rated group ideas for novelty and usefulness on separate 5-point scales. Sources: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 344), Section 3.1; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 345), Sections 3.2 and 4. The full set of experimental problem statements is not listed.
task.duration: Three rounds of three minutes each during one class session, followed by idea ratings and a questionnaire (PDF p. 4, printed p. 345, Section 4).

outcomes.name: Innovation of participants' ideas rated by the two first authors
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The two first authors rated all ideas on a five-level innovation scale adapted from Shaer et al. (2024), asking about originality and creativity relative to conventional solutions. Ideas were de-identified and shuffled within challenges. Initial Pearson r < .5; disagreements of at least 1 were discussed; final r(350) = .79, p-value < .001 (PDF p. 6, printed p. 347, Section 5.2). The paper does not specify whether the tests used separate author ratings or aggregated idea scores, which version of the idea text was rated, or the test-specific number of observations. Thus unit and n_units are null; generated-idea totals are not asserted to be the analysis N.

contrasts.reported: One-sided Mann-Whitney U test (alternative: collaborator condition greater than control): U = 2803, p-value = .8. Shapiro-Wilk: human-only WA = .85, p-valueA < .001; human and AI collaborator WB = .84, p-valueB < .001. Figure 7 shows distributions; no arm means or SDs are printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 347), Section 5.2; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 348), Section 5.2, Figure 7

outcomes.question: with_ai

The generated-idea counts were 77 in control and 76 human ideas in treatment (PDF p. 5, printed p. 346, Section 5). Section 5.2 and Figure 6 do not say whether the novelty tests use individual ratings or per-idea aggregates; unit and n_units are null.

contrasts.reported: Mann-Whitney U = 3501.5, p-value = .983. Shapiro-Wilk for human-only: WA = .95, p-valueA = .0024. Figure 6, lower panel, shows distributions; no arm means or SDs are printed.

outcomes.name: Usefulness of ideas rated by participants (results not reported)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Participants were instructed to rate every group idea for usefulness on a 5-point scale, separately from novelty (PDF p. 4, printed p. 345, Sections 3.2 and 4). eligibility.reason: Random assignment is explicitly reported for the comparison of an AI collaborator plus an AI idea editor against the same editor alone (PDF p. 5, printed p. 346, Section 4; PDF p. 3, printed p. 344, Section 3). Both arms therefore receive generative AI, and this randomized AI-configuration comparison meets criterion 1. Only 29 people were analyzed, 13 control and 16 treatment (PDF p. 5, printed p. 346, Section 5); criterion 2 is not met, irrespective of the unreported number randomized. Participants rated ideas for novelty and usefulness, and the first two authors rated innovation, meeting criterion 3 (PDF p. 4, printed p. 345, Section 3.2; PDF pp. 5-7, printed pp. 346-348, Section 5.2). The experiment remains excluded from the core dataset and listed in the screening report because it is below 50 analyzed participants. Its AI-versus-human output comparisons do not change the primary design or exclusion.

one_line_finding: Among 29 analyzed students, adding a GPT-3.5 collaborator to AI-edited group ideation yielded no significant difference in innovation (U = 2803, p = .8), novelty (U = 3501.5, p = .983), or fluency (Welch t(24.6) = 1.33, p = .2), although AI-generated ideas rated higher for innovation (U = 1629, p < .001) and novelty (U = 4463, p = .012; PDF pp. 5-7, Section 5.2, Figures 6-8).
open_questions: The randomization sentence names participants, but the procedure, relationship to existing course groups, and numbers of groups per arm are not reported (PDF pp. 4-5, Section 4). The reported course-group composition is also not consistent with the attendee total.
How many people were randomized, and did consent precede assignment? Attendance and analysis counts are reported, but assignment counts are not (PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 4-5).

Did novelty and innovation tests use individual ratings or aggregated idea scores, and how many observations entered each test? The printed reliability r(350) does not establish the analysis N, and its relationship to the reported idea totals is not explained (PDF pp. 5-7, Section 5.2).
Did the author raters score original submissions or reformulated text? The rating-spreadsheet description does not identify the version (PDF p. 6, Section 5.2).
Which human ideas entered the AI-versus-participant contrasts? Pooling across human conditions is not explicitly specified (PDF pp. 5-6, Section 5.2).
Usefulness was rated on output, but its results and comparison statistics are absent (PDF p. 4, Sections 3.2 and 4; results checked throughout the PDF).
Exact questionnaire analysis counts are not printed for the Likert items; t-test degrees of freedom are not converted into respondent counts (PDF p. 5, Section 5.1).
notes: Read all 384 markdown lines and all 10 PDF pages, including references; no appendix is present. Both raw forms parsed. Outcome matching uses construct and comparison, not the screeners' differing outcome IDs; final IDs follow A, with usefulness added as S1-O6. Equivalent wording, outcome order, and repeated facts in different fields are not counted as differences. The five originally listed comparisons are all retained. Added usefulness has no reported contrast; absence of results is not coded as a null effect. Rated-outcome units and analysis counts are null where the paper does not distinguish individual ratings from idea aggregates. The generated-idea totals and the printed r(350) are not used to infer test sample sizes. No effect sizes were calculated. The paper reports 201 ideas overall and 48 AI ideas; these are not participant counts (PDF p. 5, Section 5). No arm-specific means, SDs, effect sizes, or confidence intervals are printed; the overall fluency mean 5.3 is printed. No participant- or group-adjusted precision is described for the rating comparisons. Self-reported usability, anonymity, team-quality opinions, and open-question themes are excluded from output outcomes; Figure 5 is on PDF p. 6 (printed p. 347), not printed p. 346. No scored between-person diversity outcome or unassisted follow-up is reported. Finalization: independently read all 384 markdown lines and all 10 PDF pages, including references; no appendix is present. Python listing found no c822.*.json challenge files, so challenge_resolution is empty and all three challenge counts are zero. The seven open questions and five unresolved reconciliation differences are covered in final.open_items, with overlapping issues grouped; none affects an eligibility criterion. The original reconciliation object is preserved unchanged. The posted_data settlement route identifies data and analysis code that would be needed, not a confirmed public dataset.

differences.field: studies.S1.ai_tool.how_used: single-solution prompt versus experimental suggestions per round
differences.a: At the end of each round the AI collaborator is prompted with the problem and the group's ideas to generate a 'disruptive, and out-of-the-box solution' (max 200 characters) that is added to the pool; it suggested two ideas per round in the treatment condition (48 AI ideas in total). In both conditions an LLM idea editor reformulated every submitted idea in a neutral tone to strengthen anonymity. No control prevented participants from using other AI tools such as ChatGPT.
differences.b: At the end of each round the AI collaborator receives the problem and the other participants' ideas and generates one 'disruptive, out-of-the-box' idea (the evaluation section says two new ideas per round) that is added to the group pool, which participants see in the next round. In both arms an LLM idea editor reformulates each submitted idea into neutral language for anonymity (refinement).
differences.resolved: The prompt requests one solution per invocation, whereas the experiment explicitly supplied two suggestions each round; retain both descriptions at their stated levels.

open_items.item: Randomization procedure, allocation relative to course groups, groups per arm, and inconsistent course-group composition (open_questions[0]; PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 345-346, Section 4). Authors' allocation records and clarification of the group description would settle these details. Criterion 1 is already met by the explicit random-assignment statement; the grouping details affect design description and dependence, rather than establishing whether assignment was random.

Number randomized and whether consent preceded assignment (open_questions[1]; PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 345-346, Sections 4-5). Authors' recruitment, consent, and allocation records would settle this. Criterion 2 is based on the confirmed 29 analyzed people, not the unreported assignment count; n_randomized remains null.

Rating aggregation, statistical observation units, test-specific counts, and the relationship of r(350) to the idea totals (open_questions[2]; unresolved reconciliation differences studies.S1.outcomes.S1-O1.n_units, studies.S1.outcomes.S1-O2.unit, and studies.S1.outcomes.S1-O5.unit; PDF pp. 5-7, printed pp. 346-348, Section 5.2). Posting the analysis data and code, with idea, rater, participant, and condition identifiers, would settle these questions for both innovation and novelty comparisons. These gaps affect extraction and precision, not the established output-scoring criterion or analyzed-person count; unreported units and counts remain null.

Whether author raters scored original submissions or LLM-reformulated text (open_questions[3]; unresolved reconciliation difference open_questions.rating_text_version; PDF p. 6, printed p. 347, Section 5.2). Authors could identify the text version in the rating spreadsheet. Either version is an output of the assigned ideation workflow, so criterion 3 remains met; both arms used the AI editor (PDF pp. 3-5, Sections 3-4).

Which human ideas entered the AI-versus-participant contrasts, including whether both human conditions were pooled (open_questions[4]; PDF pp. 5-6, printed pp. 346-347, Section 5.2). Posting analysis data and code with condition and output-origin labels would identify the included ideas. These secondary output-origin contrasts do not determine eligibility of the randomized human-assistance comparison.

Unreported output-usefulness results and comparison statistics (open_questions[5]; PDF p. 4, printed p. 345, Sections 3.2 and 4; complete results checked). Authors could supply the usefulness ratings, any analysis, and the reason results were omitted. Novelty and innovation already establish criterion 3, so absent usefulness results do not change eligibility and are not coded as a null effect.

Exact questionnaire item analysis counts and missing-response handling (open_questions[6]; unresolved reconciliation difference studies.S1.participants.exclusions: questionnaire item sample sizes; PDF p. 5, printed p. 346, Section 5.1). Authors' item-level response and exclusion counts would settle this. These self-report items are separate from the confirmed 29-person creative-output sample, and their counts affect none of the three eligibility criteria; no respondent count is inferred from t-test degrees of freedom.
